$comment: Autopilot analysis rules. Edit freely; the app validates this file at startup and on every refresh. Signal types: eventId (values), errorCode (values), registryValue (name, equals), text (regex pattern), espInstallationState (equals), policyStatus (equals). Optional context: flowTags (userDriven, selfDeploying, preProvisioned, entra, hybrid, devicePreparation) and phases. When more than one rule matches the same evidence, the UI shows all of them as possible causes.

rules.likelyCause: The device is not registered with Windows Autopilot: the hardware hash was not uploaded, or the registration did not complete or was removed.
rules.recommendedFix: Check that the hardware hash is imported in Intune (Devices > Windows > Enrollment > Windows Autopilot > Devices) and that the device is assigned a deployment profile, then restart OOBE.
rules.structuralAction: Register devices through the OEM or reseller (or an automated hash-upload process) before shipping, and add a pre-deployment check that every device is registered and has an assigned profile.

verification.note: Event 807 is documented as ZtdDeviceIsNotRegistered in the Autopilot event table.

signal.description: Autopilot event 809 ZtdDeviceHasNoAssignedProfile (profile does not exist)

rules.likelyCause: The Autopilot profile assigned to the device was deleted without first being cleaned up.
rules.recommendedFix: Assign a different, existing Autopilot profile to the device, wait for the assignment to show as Assigned, then re-enroll the device.
rules.structuralAction: Change-control Autopilot profiles: never delete a profile that still has assignments. Re-target the groups to a replacement profile first.

verification.note: Documented: 'Assigned profile does not exist'.

signal.description: Autopilot event 815 ZtdDeviceHasNoAssignedProfile (no profile, no default)

rules.likelyCause: No Autopilot profile is assigned to the device and the tenant has no default profile that applies.
rules.recommendedFix: Check the device's group membership (group tag / dynamic group rule) and the profile assignments. Restart OOBE once the profile shows as Assigned.
rules.structuralAction: Use dynamic device groups based on ZTDId or group tag, and monitor devices whose profile status is not Assigned before they ship to users.

verification.note: Documented: 'No profile assigned to the device, and no default profile found in the tenant.'

rules.likelyCause: The serial number or product key recorded in Windows Autopilot doesn't match the physical hardware, for example after a motherboard replacement.
rules.recommendedFix: Deregister and re-register the device with a freshly collected hardware hash, then re-enroll.
rules.structuralAction: Add 're-register in Autopilot' as a mandatory step in the hardware repair and RMA process.

verification.note: Documented in the Autopilot event table.

signal.description: Autopilot event 171 failed to set TPM identity confirmed

rules.likelyCause: TPM attestation failed. Self-deploying and pre-provisioning modes need it.
rules.recommendedFix: Check that the device has a physical TPM 2.0 with current firmware and can reach the TPM attestation endpoints. Then retry the deployment.
rules.structuralAction: Qualify hardware models and TPM firmware versions for self-deploying and pre-provisioning before purchase, and allow the attestation endpoints through proxy and firewall.

verification.note: Documented: 'issue performing TPM attestation'. The specific root cause (firmware, network, hardware) is not stated, so confidence is medium.

signal.description: Autopilot event 172 failed to set Autopilot profile as available

rules.likelyCause: Follow-on failure that Microsoft documents as typically related to event 171 (TPM attestation).
rules.recommendedFix: Investigate event 171 and the TPM attestation prerequisites on the same device first.
rules.structuralAction: Same as TPM attestation: qualify TPM hardware and firmware, and allow the attestation endpoints.

verification.note: Documented: 'This error is typically related to event ID 171.'

rules.likelyCause: The Microsoft Entra join failed. The most common reason is Entra permissions: the user isn't allowed to join devices, or has reached the device limit.
rules.recommendedFix: In Entra ID > Devices > Device settings, check 'Users may join devices to Microsoft Entra ID' and 'Maximum number of devices per user'. Remove stale devices for the user.
rules.structuralAction: Scope device join rights to an Autopilot users group, and clean up stale Entra devices on a schedule so users don't hit the device limit.

verification.note: Microsoft documents 801C0003 as Entra join failure and permissions as the most common issue. Other causes are possible, so confidence is medium.

rules.likelyCause: MDM enrollment was refused. Common causes are a missing or incorrect Intune license for the user, or too many devices enrolled for the user.
rules.recommendedFix: Check the user's Intune license and the Intune device limit restriction, then retry enrollment.
rules.structuralAction: Assign Intune licenses through group-based licensing to every Autopilot user group, and align the Intune and Entra device limits with your device refresh cycle.

verification.note: The FAQ lists licensing and the device limit as common issues for 80180018.

signal.description: Error 0x80180014 (reuse of a self-deploying or pre-provisioned device)

rules.likelyCause: A self-deploying or pre-provisioned device is being reused, reset or redeployed while its previous Intune device record still blocks enrollment.
rules.recommendedFix: In Intune > Windows Autopilot > Devices, select the device and choose 'Unblock device' (or delete the Intune device record), then redeploy.
rules.structuralAction: Make 'delete the Intune record or unblock the device' a fixed step in the device reuse and reset runbook for self-deploying and pre-provisioned devices.

verification.note: One of two documented scenarios for 0x80180014.

rules.likelyCause: Windows (MDM) enrollment is blocked by a device platform restriction that applies to this user or device.
rules.recommendedFix: Check every Windows device platform restriction (Devices > Enrollment > Device platform restriction) and make sure Windows (MDM) is set to Allow for the groups involved.
rules.structuralAction: Document and review enrollment restrictions with group-scoped tests, so that a new restriction can't silently block Autopilot.

verification.note: Documented as 'Windows MDM enrollment is disabled in your Intune tenant' and in the Autopilot FAQ.

signal.description: Error 0x80070774 (domain controller not found or device can't join the domain)

rules.likelyCause: In a hybrid join deployment, the domain controller couldn't be reached, or the device is in a state where it can't join the domain. The most common reason is that the 'Assign user' feature was used with a hybrid profile.
rules.recommendedFix: Unassign the user from the Autopilot device, confirm the hybrid profile is assigned, and check that the device can reach a domain controller during OOBE.
rules.structuralAction: Don't use 'Assign user' with hybrid join profiles. Consider moving new deployments to Entra join to remove the DC line-of-sight dependency.

verification.note: Documented 'Error Code 80070774' section.

signal.description: Error 0x80070774 (Intune Connector for Active Directory domain mismatch)

rules.likelyCause: The Intune Connector for Active Directory is installed in a different domain than the one the domain join profile targets, or it lacks permission to create computer objects in the target OU.
rules.recommendedFix: Install or configure the connector in the matching domain. Check the ODJ connector log for event 30132 and the OU delegation for the connector account.
rules.structuralAction: Run at least two up-to-date connectors per target domain and monitor the ODJ connector service log.

verification.note: The FAQ documents the domain mismatch. The enrollment-errors page documents the ODJ privileges variant (event 30132).

rules.likelyCause: The device doesn't meet the self-deploying or pre-provisioning requirements: no physical TPM 2.0 (virtual TPM or TPM 1.2), or an unsupported Windows build. TPM attestation then times out.
rules.recommendedFix: Confirm the device has a physical TPM 2.0 and a supported Windows build. Check event 171/172 in the Autopilot event log.
rules.structuralAction: Keep a hardware compatibility list for self-deploying and pre-provisioning, and exclude virtual machines and TPM 1.2 devices from those profiles with group targeting.

verification.note: Documented 'Securing your hardware (Failed: 0x800705b4)'. 0x800705B4 is a generic timeout, so other causes are possible.

signal.description: Error 0x800705B4 (timeout) during the Enrollment Status Page

rules.likelyCause: The ESP timed out before all tracked apps and policies finished. This usually happens when the ESP timeout is too short for the number and size of required apps, or when an app hangs.
rules.recommendedFix: Check which tracked apps were still not installed when the timeout hit, and the Intune Management Extension log for a hanging install. Raise the ESP timeout or reduce the blocking app list.
rules.structuralAction: Block ESP only on a small set of essential apps, deliver the rest after ESP, and size the ESP timeout from measured install times per app.

verification.note: The ESP troubleshooting article documents timeouts caused by too many apps for the configured timeout. Mapping 0x800705B4 (ERROR_TIMEOUT) to this is an inference from context.

rules.likelyCause: A generic timeout (ERROR_TIMEOUT, Win32 error 1460). Depending on the phase this can be network or proxy latency, an unreachable service or domain controller, TPM attestation, or an ESP timeout.
rules.recommendedFix: Correlate with the phase and the Autopilot event log. Check network and proxy access to the Autopilot and Intune endpoints from the device.
rules.structuralAction: Validate the Autopilot network requirements (endpoints, proxy, SSL inspection exclusions) on every network segment used for provisioning.

verification.note: Only the meaning of the code (ERROR_TIMEOUT) is documented. Shown so the ambiguity stays visible.

rules.likelyCause: The installer reported success, but the app's detection rule doesn't match what was installed (wrong product code, version, path, or 32/64-bit registry view). Self-updating apps can also cause a version mismatch.
rules.recommendedFix: Compare the detection rule with what is actually on the device. The IntuneManagementExtension.log shows the detection result. Fix the rule and redeploy.
rules.structuralAction: Test detection rules on a reference device as part of app packaging, and avoid version-pinned detection for self-updating apps.

verification.note: Documented: 'Application installation succeeded but application is not detected', including the self-updating MSI version mismatch.

rules.likelyCause: The app was installed successfully and later uninstalled or replaced, for example by another app, a script, or a self-update, so detection fails.
rules.recommendedFix: Check the IME log and Add/Remove Programs for an uninstall or upgrade of the app after the initial install.
rules.structuralAction: Avoid overlapping deployments of the same product (an MSI LOB app and a Win32 app, or old and new versions) in the same assignment scope.

verification.note: Documented as 'deployed successfully by Intune, then subsequently uninstalled'. Less likely during ESP, so confidence is low.

rules.likelyCause: A Win32 app tracked by the ESP reported an installation error, and the ESP stops installing applications when this happens.
rules.recommendedFix: Find the Win32App_{AppID} with InstallationState 4 and check the Intune Management Extension log for that app ID's install result.
rules.structuralAction: Keep the ESP blocking app list short, test every blocking app's install command in SYSTEM context during OOBE, and monitor per-app ESP failure rates.

verification.note: Documented: 'If the value of InstallationState for any app is 4, ESP stops installing applications.'

signal.description: 'Another installation is in progress' in logs or failure details

rules.likelyCause: LOB (MSI) and Win32 apps were mixed during the ESP. Both use TrustedInstaller, which doesn't allow simultaneous installations. The Teams Machine-Wide Installer inside Microsoft 365 Apps can cause the same conflict.
rules.recommendedFix: Convert the LOB MSI apps to Win32 apps, or remove them from the ESP blocking list. Deploy Microsoft 365 Apps without Teams Machine-Wide Installer during the ESP.
rules.structuralAction: Standardize on one app type (Win32) for everything tracked by the ESP, or move to Autopilot device preparation, which supports mixing LOB and Win32 apps.

verification.note: Documented FAQ entry with this exact message.

rules.likelyCause: Another MSI installation was already running (ERROR_INSTALL_ALREADY_RUNNING). During the ESP this matches the documented LOB and Win32 app mixing conflict.
rules.recommendedFix: Check the IME log for overlapping installs, and convert the LOB MSI apps tracked by the ESP to Win32.
rules.structuralAction: Standardize on Win32 apps for everything tracked by the ESP, or move to Autopilot device preparation.

verification.note: 0x80070652 is the Windows Installer 'already running' code. The link to the documented TrustedInstaller conflict is an inference, so confidence is medium.

rules.likelyCause: The device isn't registered with Windows Autopilot, so no profile was delivered.
rules.recommendedFix: Check the registration in Intune (Windows Autopilot > Devices) by serial number. Import the hardware hash if it is missing and restart OOBE.
rules.structuralAction: Register devices through the OEM or reseller before shipping, and check registration status as part of device intake.

verification.note: One of two documented meanings of IsAutopilotDisabled = 1.

rules.likelyCause: The Autopilot profile couldn't be downloaded because of network connectivity, firewall or proxy issues, or network timeouts.
rules.recommendedFix: Check from the device during OOBE that the Autopilot deployment service endpoints are reachable, without SSL inspection. Then restart OOBE to download the profile again.
rules.structuralAction: Provide a provisioning network that meets the Autopilot networking requirements, and test it whenever proxy or firewall rules change.

verification.note: Documented: 'could also indicate that the Windows Autopilot profile couldn't be downloaded because of network connectivity or firewall issues'.

rules.likelyCause: The user signed in with an account from a different tenant than the one the device is registered with.
rules.recommendedFix: Compare AadTenantId with CloudAssignedTenantId in the same registry key. Sign in with an account from the registered tenant, or move the device registration to the right tenant.
rules.structuralAction: Customise the Entra sign-in page branding and give users clear sign-in instructions. For multi-tenant organisations, register devices in the tenant of the end user.

verification.note: Documented: 'If this registry value is 0, the user would be shown an error and forced to start over.'

signal.description: An app or policy reported 'error' in policyStatusDetails

rules.likelyCause: An app or policy targeted at the device reported an error during provisioning. If it is tracked by the ESP, it can block or fail the ESP.
rules.recommendedFix: Open the failing item and its error code in this view, then check the item's device install status in Intune and the IME log for details.
rules.structuralAction: Track per-app and per-policy failure rates across deployments, and remove unstable items from the ESP blocking list until they are fixed.

verification.note: General ESP guidance. The specific cause depends on the item's error code.
